items.speaker: Salviati
items.text:
Two research results came back, and both cut into the note's confidence, so I start by conceding.

R1 did not find Bethesda's constraint status. That is a failure of retrieval, not a negative: we do not learn that the substation is unconstrained, only that the note's "one query settles it" has not been settled. But the note already treats option 1 as the default posture and says it "passes both halves wherever a constraint exists". That is a conditional dressed up as a recommendation. The honest default is narrower. Grow behind the meter (option 5) and pay the backbone, both of which hold whatever the substation's state. The flexibility sale should be held as an unpriced option, not a revenue line. Nothing is lost by saying so, because condition 3 of the parent gate still names flexibility as a persistent value. We simply have not shown that it exists here.

R2 is more interesting, because it partly answers something the note listed as unverified. Wales has already run the community half of option 3. An application-based 100% relief for community hydro up to £50,000 rateable value was announced in 2018 and extended for 2019–20, and Ynni Ogwen was a named beneficiary. We cannot say whether it survives on the 2023 list. Even so, it changes option 3. The relief half has a Welsh precedent and may already be worth zero to the cell at the margin. What remains contested is only retention by the county, and that is exactly the half that breaks the redistributive pool. So option 3 shrinks to a single question: can new commercial capacity above a baseline be retained without taking from counties that have no wind or water? Its claim to "pass for the cell" now depends on whether that grant lapsed.

items.speaker: Sagredo
items.text:
Some of this now persuades me. The sideways finding holds up: none of the research so far has given me reason to think a level of government is the real loser. And R3 settles something useful. Wales has kept its grant-based relief for community hydro into the 2023 list, so the "exempt the community" half of option 3 already exists. That leaves option 3 as one question only: may Gwynedd keep rates from new commercial generation without taking from counties that have no rivers or hills? I think Salviati is right to shrink it that far.

On option 1, R4 is not proof, but it is a straw in the wind. The April 2025 procurement statement names no Gwynedd zone at all. Together with R1's empty hand, I would now treat the flexibility sale as something that probably does not exist here until someone shows it does.

What I am still not convinced of is the size of the thing the whole note turns on. The roofless neighbour is called the only real loser, yet the note never says how much that neighbour loses. It even lists "the network share of a typical unit rate" as unverified. If the shifted cost is a few pounds a year, the horizontal finding is true but rather unimportant, and option 2 becomes a remedy larger than the wound. If it is tens of pounds, the case for options 4 and 5 gets much stronger.

I have a second doubt about option 2. If GB Energy or Ynni Cymru pays the royalty, how is that not a grant under another name? The parent ladder forbids later rungs that lean on grants.

My two questions follow from that. How many pounds a year does one non-member household carry per cell member? And does an upstream reimburser count as grant dependence?

items.speaker: Simplicio
items.text:
Concession first: R3 beats me on option 3's relief half. Wales already runs a community hydro relief, and the note's "needs the rateable value" is now a smaller problem. But R3 also shows what that relief is: an application-based grant, with terms for 2023–24 unconfirmed. So the note's "exempt" is wrong for hydro, and the cell already leans on a discretionary Welsh Government payment.

That bears on Sagredo's second question, and I answer yes. A royalty reimbursed by GB Energy or Ynni Cymru is a subsidy. Germany's §6 worked because the EEG account was a standing, statutory, levy-funded stream. The UK has nothing like it, and the note itself shows the 2025 Budget moving levy costs to the Exchequer, where a future budget can reverse them. The Dutch history the note cites says the same: tax-route support became a subsidy. The royalty goes to the council, not the cell, but the cell is only "neutral" while the reimbursement lasts. When it stops, the asset owner pays. That is the grant dependence the ladder forbids.

On size, R5 gives no verified figure, and its unverified snippet (network about 26–29% of the cap, policy about 5–6%) does not say how much of that is recovered per kWh. The note's "cells cannot dodge the residuals" is true at the DNO-to-supplier level. How a member's bill shows them depends on the supplier's tariff design. Until someone measures it, "the only real loser" and "an unknown but material cut" are both unsupported.

Who has fewer options? The roofless would-be member. Option 5 demotes rung 5, their only door, to a top-up. Option 1 is meant to pay for that door, yet R1 and R4 found no flexibility market at Bethesda. That leaves the roofless door with no funder.

items.speaker: Salviati
items.text:
Simplicio is right three times, and the note should change each time rather than argue.

First, the county row. "Exempt" is wrong for hydro. The 2023 Regulations exempt rooftop and onsite plant. Standalone hydro stays on the list, and what it gets is an application-based Welsh Government grant (R3), whose 2023–24 terms nobody here has confirmed. The cell's rung 7 already rests on a discretionary payment, and the note should say so.

Second, the royalty. A reimbursement from GB Energy or Ynni Cymru is a subsidy while it lasts. My repair is to make the asset owner's duty contingent: the royalty is payable only out of reimbursement actually received, and it falls to zero the moment reimbursement stops. The asset owner can then never be worse off than today. No rung's rationale depends on the money, so the ladder's grant rule is not breached. The risk sits with the community council, which today receives nothing, so it loses no option either. That is weaker than §6 EEG, but it is honest.

Third, the roofless door. Option 5 as written does narrow it, and option 1 cannot fund it, since R1 and R4 found no market. The repair is to fund the door from inside rung 5. Use the Italian split the note already praises: shared kWh pay their own cost-reflective network share. The roofless member then shifts nothing onto non-members and needs no outside funder. The cost is smaller savings, not a closed door.

On size, I concede to Sagredo. R5 is unverified and R6 failed, so "the only real loser" stays unsized. The finding should be stated as the only line with a loser, magnitude not yet measured.

Only standalone assets… are rated" with a statement that standalone community hydro is rated but may receive an application-based 100% Welsh Government grant up to £50,000 RV (R3), with 2023–24 terms unconfirmed.

In option 2's Design, add: "The royalty is payable only from reimbursement received and lapses to zero if reimbursement ends, so the asset owner never pays net." Rewrite its Verdict to say it passes the asset-owner half unconditionally and the council half only while funded.

In option 5, replace "treat through-grid matching as the top-up layer" with "keep rung 5 open as of right, with shared kWh paying their cost-reflective network share (the Italian CER split), so the roofless door needs no flexibility revenue". In "The finding first", change "the only line in the ledger with a real loser" to "the only line with a loser; its size is not yet measured".

items.speaker: Sagredo
items.text:
Some of this now persuades me. Salviati's corrections to the county row are plainly right: standalone hydro sits on a discretionary grant, not an exemption, and the note should say so. I also accept stating the sideways finding as "the only line with a loser, size not yet measured". That claim is honest, though it is now a much weaker one than the note's headline.

I am not yet persuaded by either repair, for reasons that mirror each other.

On the contingent royalty: if it is payable only from reimbursement received, the asset owner is safe. But the council's income then depends entirely on GB Energy or Ynni Cymru choosing to pay. That is simply a grant to the community council, routed through a hydro meter. Why the wrapper? What does a per-kWh royalty do that a direct fuel-poverty grant to the council would not? If the answer is "it ties the money to local generation and so to consent", I can see that. But the note should say it, because otherwise option 2 looks like decoration on a subsidy.

On the roofless door: making shared kWh pay their own cost-reflective network share keeps the door open. But I do not know whether anything worthwhile is left behind it. If the network share is most of the saving, a roofless member joins for very little. And this split covers only network charges, not the per-kWh levies, which would still shift. I also do not know whether any GB supplier arrangement would let a cell pay such a share at all. Italy has a mechanism for it, and I have not heard that we do.

So my questions are two. After that split, what does a roofless rung-5 member actually save per year? And is there any existing UK route by which a cell could pay a cost-reflective network share for shared kWh?

items.speaker: Simplicio
items.text:
Salviati's contingent royalty does protect the asset owner, and I concede that. It cannot leave the owner worse off than today. But Sagredo's question stands, and the answer is that it is a grant to the council with a hydro meter attached. If the only reason for the wrapper is consent and the tie to local generation, the note should say so, and it should stop calling option 2 a "design already working somewhere". Germany's §6 worked because the money came from a statutory account. Nothing in the note or R1–R6 shows a UK equivalent.

The roofless-door repair has a bigger hole. The Italian split works in Italy because Italian law built a mechanism for it. For GB, I am confident of one public fact: distribution charges are billed to the supplier, who passes them through in the customer's tariff. A cell with no licence has no obvious way to pay a separate network share for its shared kWh. Neither the note nor any research result shows one. Without a mechanism, "shared kWh pay their own share" is a wish.

The repair also does not deliver "shifts nothing". It covers network charges only. The per-kWh levies still move onto non-members, as the note itself says. And R5 could not even show how much of a unit rate is per-kWh. So nobody can yet say what a roofless member saves after the split, and Sagredo's first question is still unanswered. If the answer is pennies, the door is open in name only.

So the party left with fewer options is still the roofless would-be member. Option 5 demotes their only route, and the repair funding it has no mechanism and no figure. The note should keep rung 5 at full standing until someone shows what lies behind it. Demoting it before then removes an option on the strength of an assumption.

The whole note is a single-seat desk pass with no independent adversary and has not been through the gate.

# The ratchet cell's governance ledger — what each level gives up, and where every level gains

_Published live (2026-11-09). A follow-on to the ratchet cell (`NOTES-ratchet-cell.md`). The question: as a cell climbs its ladder, what does it take from each level of governance, from community council to the UN — VAT, levies, network charges, business rates, grid upkeep? And which designs, already working somewhere, let every level gain more than it gives up? This is a desk pass by one agent: about a dozen sourced lookups, no fleet and no independent adversary seat. Each option carries its own adversary, but the run has not been through the gate. Figures marked ≈ are orders of magnitude, not models._

_Moved on 2026-11-09 by a [world computer run](/world-computer?run=run-001): standalone hydro is rated but can get a discretionary Welsh grant rather than an exemption; the flexibility sale is now held back until Bethesda's constraint status is known; the royalty is made contingent on reimbursement; rung 5 stays open as of right; and the roofless neighbour's loss is marked as unmeasured._

---

## The finding first: the loser is the roofless neighbour, not a level of government

Go through the ledger level by level and something unexpected appears. **Most levels of governance lose little or nothing to a ratchet cell, and several gain.** The real cost of the cell falls sideways, not upwards. It lands on the household with no roof, no share and no club place, which ends up carrying a larger share of the fixed system costs that cell members stop paying per kWh. The walls ledger in the parent note already lists this as *network-cost shifting: political contest*. This pass gives it its proper place. It is the only line with a loser; its size is not yet measured. That loser is not a government.

So "every level gains" is the wrong test, or at least only half of it. It mostly passes already. The test that bites is **every level gains *and* the non-participant is no worse off.** The options below are scored on both halves.

## The ledger — what a cell takes, level by level

The take comes in three kinds, and they should never be added together: a **fiscal loss** (money a government no longer receives), a **reallocation** (a revenue-capped cost that moves onto other bill-payers), and a **gain**.

| Level | What a cell touches | Kind | Size and sign |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Community council** (Cyngor Cymuned) | Nothing. The precept is unaffected. | — | Zero take. Possible gain: a council roof can host a rung-3 lease, and the council can hold or channel a benefit fund. |
| **County** (Gwynedd) | Non-domestic rates on standalone generation (hydro, ground-mount); planning. Rates are pooled nationally in Wales, so the county keeps nothing directly. | Fiscal, small | Rooftop and onsite plant has been **exempt from Welsh rates since 1 April 2024, to 31 March 2035** (Valuation for Rating (Plant and Machinery) (Wales) (Amendment) Regs 2023), so the roof rungs take nothing from rates. Standalone assets (rung 7's hydro, any ground-mount) stay rated. Standalone community hydro is **not exempt**, but it may receive an application-based 100% Welsh Government grant up to £50,000 rateable value ([R3](https://www.gov.wales/non-domestic-business-rates-support-community-owned-hydropower-projects-2022-2023)). Guidance exists for 2023–24, but its terms are unconfirmed. Gains: lower energy bills in its own schools and buildings, fewer fuel-poor households. |
| **Welsh Government** | The rates pool; Ynni Cymru grant spend (rung 0). Energy licensing is **reserved**, so there is no tax or levy lever here. | Spend in, target out | A net gainer against its own target of **1.5 GW locally owned by 2035**. Every cell is cheap delivery of a stated objective. |
| **UK Treasury** | VAT at 5% on every displaced kWh; 0% VAT on solar installs (to March 2027); income tax on share interest; CBS corporation tax; the share of the Renewables Obligation it now funds. | Fiscal loss, partly offset | VAT forgone ≈ **£25 a year per member household** displacing ~2,000 kWh at ~26p. Offsets: taxable share interest, employment taxes on the paid officer, and lower fuel-poverty spend. Probably net-negative but small. Not modelled. |
| **Ofgem / DNO** (SP Energy Networks, North Wales) | Distribution and transmission charges per kWh. | **Reallocation** | The DNO loses **nothing**: allowed revenue is set by the price control (RIIO-ED2), so lower volume raises unit tariffs for everyone else. The transmission and distribution *residuals* already moved to banded fixed charges under the 2022 Targeted Charging Review, so cells cannot dodge them at the DNO-to-supplier level. How a member's bill shows them depends on the supplier's tariff design. What cells still avoid is the per-kWh, cost-reflective part. The **gain** is flexibility: a cell battery or diverter that defers reinforcement is cheaper than copper, and the DNO keeps part of any underspend under its totex incentive. |
| **Policy levies** (RO, FiT, CfD, ECO, Warm Home Discount) | Per-kWh levies on supplied energy. | **Reallocation** | The total cost is fixed (certificates and contracts are owed whatever the volume), so a cell shifts levy onto non-members. **This contest shrank in April 2026.** The 2025 Budget ended ECO on bills and moved **75% of domestic RO cost to the Exchequer** for 2026–29 (≈£150 a year off the average bill combined; ≈£90 from RO alone, per the government factsheet). That moves cost from a regressive base (per kWh) to a progressive one (general taxation). It is the largest single cut to the cell's sideways take so far, and it happened for reasons unrelated to cells. |
| **EU** | Nothing. The UK is outside; ETS linking and CBAM do not reach a domestic cell. | — | Precedent library only (see options). |
| **UN** (UNFCCC, SDG 7) | Nothing. | — | Takes nothing and can give nothing a cell can spend. Its only currency is attributable mitigation in the UK's NDC, which cells add to at no cost to it. |

**Read it upward:** above the UK there is nothing to negotiate. **Read it at the UK:** the Treasury's loss is VAT-sized and small. The DNO's is zero by construction. **Read it sideways:** the real contest is levy and network reallocation onto non-members, and the 2026 levy move has already cut it, by an amount not yet measured.

## The options

Each one is a design already running somewhere, mapped onto the cell's levels, scored on both halves of the test, and set against its strongest adversary.

### 1. Pay the backbone, sell the flexibility — the network level gains by buying what the cell can do

**Design.** The cell does not try to avoid network costs it causes. Members keep paying the fixed residuals (the 2022 Targeted Charging Review already makes that compulsory), and the cell volunteers a capacity-based contribution for any through-grid sharing (rung 5). The cell then *sells* to SP Energy Networks what it is physically good at: diverters and anchor batteries (rungs 1 and 6) bid into the DNO's flexibility tenders for the local substation, getting paid to defer reinforcement.

**Who gains.** DNO: deferral is cheaper than reinforcement, and it keeps part of the underspend. Non-members: lower reinforcement cost in their tariffs, and no residual shifted onto them. Cell: a new revenue line built on persistent value, which is exactly what condition 3 of the parent gate demanded ("price off self-consumption, avoided-network and flexibility value — the parts that persist").

**Precedents.** SPEN runs flexibility tenders across North Wales through Piclo/ElectronConnect: 113 MW secured at 12 HV/EHV sites in north-west England and North Wales in one earlier round. Italy's renewable energy communities (CER) reimburse only the *cost-reflective* network component on shared energy, not the residual. That is the right split. Germany's new energy sharing (§42c EnWG, live 1 June 2026) deliberately gives **no** network-charge reduction, on the grounds that shared electrons still use the wires.

**Adversary.** The tenders are thin and pitched at the wrong voltage. SPEN's 2025 round contracted **13.84 MW of 56 MW tendered**, mostly at HV/EHV. Low-voltage contracts, the voltage where a valley cell sits, are new and rare. Unless the Bethesda substation is actually constrained, there is nothing to sell, and the value per kWh may be pennies. Worse, Ofgem's *Energy System Cost Allocation and Recovery Review* (call for input closed September 2025) may push more cost onto standing charges, which cuts the unit-rate savings that rungs 2 and 5 run on. **Verdict:** passes both halves if the substation is constrained. Otherwise it is a posture with no revenue. One query to SPEN's constraint maps settles which, and that query has not yet succeeded (see next steps).

### 2. A per-kWh royalty to the community council, reimbursed from above — the German §6 shape

**Design.** Large cell assets (the rung-7 hydro, any rung-3 anchor roof over a threshold) pay a small per-kWh royalty to the community council. The council uses its general power of competence to spend it on the fuel-poor cohort the parent gate found the ladder cannot reach (the "false for the acute fuel-poverty cohort" clause). The decisive feature is borrowed exactly: **the royalty is reimbursed by the level above**, so the asset owner is neutral, the community council gains, and the payer is the level that wants consent and build rate. The royalty is payable only from reimbursement received and lapses to zero if reimbursement ends, so the asset owner never pays net. In substance this is a grant to the council, paid through a generation meter. The only reason for the per-kWh wrapper is that it ties the money to local generation, and so to consent.

**Precedents.** Germany, §6 EEG: operators may pay affected municipalities up to **0.2 ct/kWh**, and for EEG-subsidised plants the grid operator reimburses it. In effect the national surcharge account pays the municipality. Since the 2024 EEErtrBetG, projects approved after 31 December 2024 must pay (0.2 ct/kWh wind, 0.1 ct/kWh ground-mount PV, up to 0.4 ct/kWh for wind by agreement). The UK has now built its own version for consent: the **Bill Discount Scheme** gives households within 500 m of 43 new transmission projects £250 a year for ten years from 2027, funded by every bill-payer at roughly 80p–£2 a year. Wales keeps a register of community benefit (the £5k/MW onshore wind norm). None of these is a UK statutory account of the §6 kind. The German shape has no working UK equivalent yet.

**Who gains.** Community council: income it has never had, ring-fenced to the cohort the ladder fails. County and Welsh Government: progress on the fuel-poverty and local-ownership targets. Nation: social licence. Non-members: if the royalty pays for fuel-poverty outreach, the most exposed non-participants are the ones who gain.

**Adversary.** The UK has no EEG account. If nobody above reimburses, there is no royalty, and a reimbursement from GB Energy or Ynni Cymru is a subsidy for as long as it lasts. A future budget can end it, as it could reverse the 2026 levy move. Scale is honest but small: 0.2p × a 100 kW hydro's ≈400 MWh is ≈**£800 a year**. That is a real outreach budget for one valley, but no more. And the community council is itself run by unpaid volunteers, so the parent note's "residual saint" moves rather than disappears. **Verdict:** passes the asset-owner half unconditionally, because the owner never pays net, and no rung's rationale depends on the money. It passes the council half only while it is funded. The candidate funder is Great British Energy's community fund or Ynni Cymru, paying the royalty rather than the capex. If funding stops, the council falls back to today's position of zero.

### 3. Exempt the community, retain the commercial — the county finally holds a stake

**Design.** Split the rates treatment of standalone generation by ownership. Community-owned assets (CBS, asset-locked) get full relief. Commercial generation in the same county pays rates, and the county **retains** them instead of pooling them. Gwynedd gains real income from the big commercial projects it hosts, the cell's rung-7 assets pay nothing, and the Welsh pool loses only the small rates bill on community assets.

**Precedents, one per nation.** *Scotland:* Renewable Energy Generation Relief gives community-owned schemes (≥15% of annual profit to a community organisation) 100% relief up to £145k rateable value, tapering above. *England:* the Non-Domestic Rating (Renewable Energy Projects) Regulations 2013 let councils keep rates from designated renewable projects, protected from the April 2026 retention reset. *Wales:* onsite plant has been exempt since April 2024, so the roof half is already done. For standalone hydro, the Welsh Government has run an application-based 100% rates relief for community hydro up to £50,000 rateable value. It was announced in 2018 and extended for 2019–20, with Ynni Ogwen named as a beneficiary ([R2](https://www.gov.wales/100-rates-relief-community-hydro-projects); [extension](https://www.gov.wales/100-business-rate-relief-continue-flow-community-hydro-projects)). Its status on the 2023 list is unconfirmed: guidance pages exist up to 2023–24, but those terms were not read (R3, cited in the ledger). *Spain:* municipalities may voluntarily waive up to **50% of IBI** (property tax) and **95% of ICIO** (works tax) on solar installs. Many do, so the lowest level gives up tax by choice, because the local return is worth more to it.

**Who gains.** County: a retained income it lacks today. Welsh Government: delivery of the 1.5 GW target at the cost of a small slice of the pool. Cell: cheaper rung-7 assets. Non-members: neutral to slightly positive (council income).

**Adversary.** Wales pools non-domestic rates *on purpose*: it is redistributive. Letting resource-rich counties keep generation rates takes from the counties without wind or water. That is zero-sum inside Wales, which is the very move the option claims to avoid. England's retention mostly produced nothing, because the de facto onshore wind ban followed straight after. And a small community hydro may already sit under small business rates relief, so the relief half could be worth zero. The Spanish evidence cuts both ways: 38% of municipalities offer no IBI bonus at all. **Verdict:** the community-relief half already exists in Wales as a discretionary grant, so it adds little that is new. The one open question is whether Gwynedd can **retain rates from new commercial capacity only**, above a baseline, as England designed it, without taking from counties that have no wind or water. Unless retention is limited in that way, the option fails at Wales level. The Ogwen hydro's rateable value is still unpriced, because the VOA entry was not retrieved (R2).

### 4. Move the take from the bill to the tax base — the Dutch fiscal route, and why it was abandoned

**Design.** Close the sideways contest at the root. The cost a cell shifts onto non-members is whatever is recovered *per kWh* without being caused per kWh: levies and network residuals. Every pound moved from that base to general taxation shrinks the cell's take from its roofless neighbour, and a tax base is progressive where a per-kWh charge is regressive. The cell-specific version adds a published **fiscal ledger** for each cell: VAT forgone set against taxes paid (share interest, wages, CBS corporation tax) and fuel-poverty spend avoided, so the Treasury can see its own balance.

**Precedents.** *UK, already moving:* the 2025 Budget took ECO off bills and 75% of domestic RO cost into the Exchequer for 2026–29, under the Energy Independence Bill. *Netherlands:* the **postcoderoosregeling** (to March 2021) gave cooperative members in neighbouring postcodes a reduced energy-tax rate on their share of the cooperative's output. It was a direct Treasury-to-cell fiscal transfer. It was **replaced by a subsidy** (the SCE, from April 2021) because the fiscal route was complex and hard to target, and the first SCE round was fully allocated in about two months, which is waitlist evidence. *Belgium (Flanders):* the meter-that-runs-backwards was struck down in 2021 precisely as a regressive cross-subsidy. That is the counter-precedent this option exists to avoid.

**Who gains.** Non-members: most of all, because the shift onto them shrinks. Treasury: neutral-to-negative, but now *visible*, and the per-cell ledger turns an argument into arithmetic. Cell: unaffected or slightly negative (smaller per-kWh savings), which is exactly the spread compression the parent template already designs around.

**Adversary.** This option is mostly a description of what is already happening, plus a ledger. The RO transfer is time-limited (to 2028–29), and a future budget can reverse it. The Dutch history says tax-route support for cells gets converted into subsidy once it grows, and subsidy is the grant-dependence the ladder is built to avoid ("no later rung's rationale cites grants"). The fiscal ledger is unvalidated, and an honest one may show a net Treasury loss. **Verdict:** the strongest on the non-member half and the weakest on the Treasury half. Its real value is defensive: it puts a number on the "regressive cells" attack before someone else does.

### 5. The frame-breaker: share the electrons without sharing the wires

**Design.** Stop asking how to compensate the levels the cell takes from, and push value down the ladder towards rungs that take nothing. Behind-the-meter and private-wire rungs (1, 2, 3 and anchor batteries) use no public network for the shared kWh, so they shift no network cost at all. Through-grid sharing (rung 5) is where the reallocation lives. Reorder the cell's growth plan so its expansion comes mainly from roofs, diverters, private wires and behind-the-meter storage. Keep rung 5 open as of right, with shared kWh paying their cost-reflective network share (the Italian CER split), so the roofless door needs no flexibility revenue.

**Precedent.** The physics, and the German legislator's reading of it: §42c gives through-grid sharing no network relief *because* it uses the network. Italy, Spain and Austria went the other way and discount shared kWh, which buys uptake at the cost of the sideways shift. Bethesda's own evidence points the same way: the binding constraint is *generation supply*, not demand. The missing rungs are roofs, which are behind the meter by design.

**Who gains.** Every level, almost trivially, because almost nothing is taken. Non-members: not harmed by behind-the-meter self-consumption beyond its levy share, which the 2026 move has shrunk.

**Adversary.** Self-consumption is still volume that does not pay per-kWh levies, so the sideways shift shrinks but never reaches zero. More seriously, behind-the-meter value goes only to people with roofs, private wires or anchor hosts, which is exactly the equity residue the parent gate found. Rung 5 is how a roofless member joins. The Italian split repairs this only in part, and three gaps remain. It covers network charges, not per-kWh levies, which still shift. No GB route has been shown by which a cell without a supply licence could pay a separate network share for shared kWh, since distribution charges are billed to the supplier. And nobody has yet measured what a roofless member still saves after the split. **Verdict:** the cleanest answer to the governance question and still the weakest on equity. Its job is as a dial, not a doctrine: grow behind the meter by default, and keep through-grid membership open at full standing as the roofless door. Do not demote it until someone shows what lies behind that door.

## What I think

The question assumed the fight was vertical: parish against county against Westminster. The ledger says it is horizontal. Above the UK nothing is taken. At the UK level the Treasury's loss is VAT-sized and the DNO's is zero by design. The real cost lands on non-participating bill-payers, and it is already shrinking for reasons unrelated to cells (the 2022 residual reform, the 2026 levy move). **My read: option 5 plus the backbone half of option 1 is the default. The flexibility sale is a held option, unpriced until Bethesda's constraint status is known (R1: not retrievable from SPEN's data in this pass).** **Option 2 is the one worth campaigning for**, because it is the only design that turns a level of government into the *funder* of the fuel-poverty cohort the ladder cannot reach. It needs exactly one thing the UK lacks, an upstream reimburser, and GB Energy's community programme is the obvious candidate. Option 3 is good for Gwynedd but breaks the Welsh pool, so it only works in its English, new-capacity-only form. Option 4 is a defensive ledger to keep in a drawer, not a strategy.

## What I would do next

1. **One lookup that decides option 1:** SPEN's network capacity and constraint map for the Bethesda primary substation. Constrained means a flexibility line exists. Unconstrained means option 1 is posture only. The first attempt failed on a tool limit ([R1](https://www.spenergynetworks.co.uk/userfiles/file/dg_heat_maps_overview.pdf)). The April 2025 procurement statement names no Bethesda or Gwynedd zone, but the Market Prospectus and the tender-zone data were not opened ([R4](https://www.spenergynetworks.co.uk/userfiles/file/SPEN_2025_C31E_Procurement_Statement.pdf)). A non-answer must not be read as "unconstrained".
2. **One number that prices option 3:** the rateable value (or rates exemption status) of Ynni Ogwen's hydro, from the VOA list. The first attempt could not open the entry (R2).
3. **Ask the Germany question in the UK:** whether GB Energy's community fund or Ynni Cymru would reimburse a per-kWh community-council royalty in place of a capex grant. It is the cheapest design here that discharges the fuel-poverty clause. *Outward-facing, so Tom's call.*
4. **Size the sideways loser and the roofless door:** how many pounds a year one non-member carries per cell member, what a rung-5 member saves after paying a cost-reflective network share, and whether any GB route lets a cell pay that share. R5 found no verified figure, and R6 failed to fetch.
5. **Run this through the gate.** This was a single-seat desk pass. Option 2 especially needs an independent adversary before it climbs.

## Sources checked in this pass

German §6 EEG and the 2024 EEErtrBetG (Taylor Wessing, gesetze-im-internet); §42c EnWG energy sharing (Gleiss Lutz, Görg, cleanthinking); Italian CER grant and tariff (ReScoop, Advant NCTM, ANCE — the base €/MWh tariff was **not** found, so it is not quoted); Welsh onsite-plant rates exception (WSI 2023/1229, gov.wales); Scottish Renewable Energy Generation Relief (mygov.scot and council pages); English renewable-project rates retention (SI 2013, gov.uk retention reset 2026); Spanish IBI/ICIO bonuses (fiscal-impuestos, selectra, interempresas); Dutch postcoderoos to SCE (solarmagazine, officielebekendmakingen); UK 2025 Budget levy moves (gov.uk Energy Independence Bill factsheet, Cornwall Insight); Bill Discount Scheme (gov.uk); SPEN flexibility tenders (SPEN C31E procurement reports); Welsh 1.5 GW local-ownership target (gov.wales, Regen).

Added by the run: R1, SPEN DG heat-map methodology (https://www.spenergynetworks.co.uk/userfiles/file/dg_heat_maps_overview.pdf), with Bethesda's status not found; R2, Welsh community hydro rates relief (https://www.gov.wales/100-rates-relief-community-hydro-projects, https://www.gov.wales/100-business-rate-relief-continue-flow-community-hydro-projects), with the VOA entry not found; R3, the relief's continuation (https://www.gov.wales/low-carbon-energy, https://www.gov.wales/non-domestic-business-rates-support-community-owned-hydropower-projects-2022-2023); R4, SPEN 2025 C31E procurement statement (https://www.spenergynetworks.co.uk/userfiles/file/SPEN_2025_C31E_Procurement_Statement.pdf), with no Gwynedd zone named; R5, Ofgem price cap April 2026 (https://www.ofgem.gov.uk/news/changes-energy-price-cap-between-1-april-and-30-june-2026, https://www.ofgem.gov.uk/sites/default/files/2026-06/Summary-of-changes-to-energy-price-cap-1-July-to-30-September-2026.pdf).

**Partly verified (R2, R3):** a current Welsh hydro-specific rates relief. It exists as an application-based grant up to 2023–24, but those terms are unconfirmed.

**Not verified, so not relied on:** Austria's energy-community network discounts (named only as a direction above); the network share of a typical unit rate (R5 gives only an unverified snippet of about 26–29% network and 5–6% policy cost in the cap, from an unknown table, and does not say how much is recovered per kWh; R6 failed); any GB mechanism for a cell to pay a network share on shared kWh.

---
